current_activity: lands on Gold Beach near Hable de Heurtot as the right-flank reserve brigade of the 50th Division
notes: Event date: 6 June 1944, about noon (Ellis, vol. I, p. 178: about an hour after the 151st Brigade began landing at about eleven). Event definition: The brigade, the second reserve brigade of the 50th Division in the Gold assault, starts landing about noon near Hable de Heurtot instead of on Jig beach, to avoid fire from le Hamel (Ellis, p. 178); by the night its leading troops have passed la Rosière and turned south astride the Bayeux road, the South Wales Borderers securing the Aure bridge at Vaux-sur-Aure (p. 210). Wikipedia says the brigade formed the right flank of the 50th Division on Gold Beach. Event support: two source families (Ellis, the British official history, and Wikipedia). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, pp. 178-179: "About an hour later the 56th Brigade started landing near Hable de Heurtot so as to avoid fire from le Hamel"; pp. 210-211: "Leading troops of the 56th Brigade had also passed through la Rosiére and turned southwards astride the road to Bayeux"; Wikipedia, 56th Infantry Brigade (United Kingdom): "where it formed the right flank of the 50th (Northumbrian) Infantry Division on Gold Beach". Location: Gold Beach (PL0156) with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is the Gold Beach sector; the landing place, Hable de Heurtot, and the night positions inland are not separate places in the dataset. Location support: Ellis names Hable de Heurtot on the Gold beaches (p. 178); Wikipedia names Gold Beach. Context: Relationship: attached to the 50th Division from the landing (Wikipedia: attached to the 50th Division until 10 June); XXX Corps as the 50th Division's corps, with the row date as start (inferred value).

current_activity: takes Bayeux, then holds defensive positions blocking the approaches from Caumont and Saint-Lô
notes: Event date: 7 June 1944 (Ellis, vol. I, p. 231: "on the 7th"; Wikipedia: 7 June). Event definition: The brigade takes Bayeux on 7 June, leaving the town mainly intact, and occupies defensive positions blocking the approaches from Caumont and Saint-Lô; it then captures Sully on the Drôme but cannot take the enemy's main defences west of the river (Ellis, p. 231; Wikipedia). Event support: two source families (Ellis, the British official history, and Wikipedia). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 231: "The 56th Brigade on its right had taken Bayeux (on the 7th)"; Wikipedia, 56th Infantry Brigade (United Kingdom): "liberated Bayeux on 7 June leaving the town mainly intact". Location: Bayeux (PL0033) with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the point is the town; the defensive positions blocking its approaches lay round it. Location support: Ellis and Wikipedia both say the brigade took Bayeux on 7 June.

current_activity: commands a tank-infantry group that fights into the middle of Tilly-sur-Seulles; withdrawn at dark
notes: Event date: 11 June 1944 (Ellis, vol. I, p. 252). Event definition: With the 7th Armoured Division's attack stalled, two tank-infantry groups are formed on 11 June; the first, under command of the brigade, renews the attack on Tilly-sur-Seulles and fights into the middle of the town by evening, but the tanks fail to get round the flank and the group is withdrawn when it grows dark (Ellis, p. 252). On the afternoon of 12 June, when the 7th Armoured Division moves off with its own lorried brigade, the brigade reverts to the 50th Division (p. 254). Wikipedia says all its battalions were involved in the taking of Tilly-sur-Seulles. Event support: two source families (Ellis, the British official history, and Wikipedia). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 252: "the first, under command of 56th Infantry Brigade to renew the attack on Tilly sur Seulles"; "At Tilly the 56th fought their way into the middle of the town by the evening"; p. 254: "the 56th Brigade reverted to the 50th Division"; Wikipedia, 56th Infantry Brigade (United Kingdom): "It remained attached to the 50th Division until 10 June, after which it was attached to the 7th Armoured Division until 12 June". Location: Tilly-sur-Seulles (PL0349) with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the point is the town, which the brigade fought into; it was withdrawn at dark. Location support: Ellis names the town (p. 252). Context: Relationship: the 7th Armoured Division attachment is dated by the sources, 11 to 12 June (Ellis pp. 252 and 254; Wikipedia gives from 10 June); the earlier attachment to the 50th Division is closed the day before (inferred value).

current_activity: opens Bluecoat with the 231st Brigade; clears the Saint-Germain-d'Ectot ridge but is stopped on the forward slopes
notes: Event date: 30 July 1944, about six in the morning (Ellis, vol. I, p. 388; the day is the opening of Bluecoat, p. 392: "during the 30th"). Event definition: XXX Corps opens Operation Bluecoat at about six in the morning with the 231st and 56th Brigade Groups of the 50th Division; the brigade makes less headway than the 231st: the Saint-Germain-d'Ectot ridge, a short distance from the start, holds several German platoon localities, and once they are cleared every attempt to advance down the forward slopes is stopped by the enemy on another ridge less than a mile away (Ellis, pp. 388-389). Wikipedia lists actions north of Saint-Germain-d'Ectot. Event support: two source families (Ellis, the British official history, and Wikipedia). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 388: "On the left XXX Corps led off at about six o'clock in the morning with the 231st and 56th Brigade Groups from the 50th Division"; p. 389: "On their right the 56th Brigade made less headway"; p. 392: "during the 30th"; Wikipedia, 56th Infantry Brigade (United Kingdom): "Later actions were north of St Germain d'Ectot". Location: Saint-Germain-d'Ectot, Calvados (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the point is the village; the brigade fought on the ridge by it and on its forward slopes. Location support: Ellis names the Saint-Germain-d'Ectot ridge (p. 389).

current_activity: under the 59th Division, follows the German withdrawal to the Orne upstream of Grimbosq, near Thury-Harcourt
notes: Event date: 5 August 1944, nightfall (Ellis, vol. I, p. 408). Event definition: In the German withdrawal before XII Corps, by nightfall on 5 August the 59th Division, with the 34th Tank Brigade and the brigade under command, has reached the Orne upstream of the 53rd Division; from the loop in the Orne near Thury-Harcourt the British line bends back westwards (Ellis, p. 408). Wikipedia says the brigade came under the 59th Division in early August and lists the liberation of Thury-Harcourt. Event support: two source families (Ellis, the British official history, and Wikipedia). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 408: "the 59th Division (with 34th Tank Brigade and 56th Infantry Brigade under command) had reached the river further upstream"; Wikipedia, 56th Infantry Brigade (United Kingdom): "came under command of the 59th (Staffordshire) Infantry Division in early August 1944"; "the liberation of Thury-Harcourt in the Suisse Normande". Location: Thury-Harcourt (PL0347) with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is the town at the Orne loop; the division's front on the river is not located more closely. Location support: Ellis names the Orne loop near Thury-Harcourt (p. 408).

current_activity: becomes an integral part of the 49th (West Riding) Division, replacing the 70th Brigade; end of its independent period
notes: Event date: 20 August 1944 (Ellis, vol. I, p. 523: "from 20.8.44"; Wikipedia: on 20 August). Event definition: The brigade becomes an integral part of the 49th Division, replacing the 70th Brigade, which was broken up after heavy losses (Ellis, vol. I, Appendix IV, pp. 523 and 528; Wikipedia). This ends its period as an independent brigade; the later rows of its history belong to the division. Event support: two source families (Ellis, the British official history, and Wikipedia). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 523: "Became integral part of the"; "49th Division from 20.8.44"; pp. 528-529: "56th Brigade (from 20.8.44)"; Wikipedia, 56th Infantry Brigade (United Kingdom): "On 20 August the brigade was permanently attached to the 49th (West Riding) Infantry Division"; "The brigade replaced the 70th Brigade". Location: the dataset place Caen sector (representative point) with a precision of 25 km. Location approximate: a representative point: the sources give the change but not where the brigade was. Location support: no source read places the brigade on the day; the point is the Caen sector, east of which I Corps (with the 49th Division) was advancing. Context: Relationship: organic to the 49th Division from 20 August 1944 (dated by Ellis and Wikipedia); the attachment to the 59th Division and the XII Corps relation are closed on 19 August (inferred value: old value no end, new value 19 August, reason the change of 20 August).
